research_material:
I make a timetable every Sunday and quit by Tuesday
how do you study when your phone is right there
I always plan too much and then feel behind by Wednesday
does anyone actually stick to a study schedule or is it a scam
I redo my planner every week instead of actually studying

pain_points: Over-planning without execution (planner becomes procrastination tool)
Skepticism about whether study schedules actually work
Perfectionism loop: redoing systems instead of doing the work

ideas.idea: Tuesday Breakdown: Why your Sunday plan dies by midweek + what actually sticks (micro-adjustments instead of total rewrites)
ideas.unique_angle: Most advice assumes the plan fails because students are lazy—actually naming the specific day the failure happens and treating it as a predictable pattern, not a character flaw

ideas.idea: Reel: 'Day 1 vs Day 3 of my study schedule' (exaggerated comparison of effort invested in planning vs actual studying)
ideas.unique_angle: Using humor to expose the emotional investment in the plan vs the reality of execution without shame

ideas.idea: The Phone Proximity Problem: practical phone-away setups that don't require willpower (physical barriers, not motivation)
ideas.unique_angle: Treating phone distraction as an environmental design problem, not a discipline problem

ideas.idea: Carousel: 'Phone spots that actually worked' (student-submitted locations, not generic library advice)
ideas.unique_angle: Crowdsourced real solutions from the audience instead of prescriptive expert tips

ideas.idea: Poll/quiz: 'Is your planner a study tool or a procrastination tool?' + reframe planning as the enemy (not the solution)
ideas.unique_angle: Directly naming that planners can be avoidance behavior, validating the audience's suspicion instead of selling them more planning

ideas.idea: Post: 'Your planner doesn't need a redesign, your schedule does' (distinguish between aesthetic tweaking and strategy tweaking)
ideas.unique_angle: Separating the emotional satisfaction of a pretty planner from actual productivity

ideas.idea: Honest testimonial: 'I asked 20 students if they stick to schedules—here's what they actually said' (no fluff, raw answers)
ideas.pain_point: Skepticism about whether study schedules actually work
ideas.unique_angle: Instead of defending scheduling, amplifying the doubt and showing nuanced truths from real students

ideas.idea: Reel: Study schedule fails ranked (from 'lasted 3 days' to 'lasted 1 study session') with what they learned each time
ideas.pain_point: Skepticism about whether study schedules actually work
ideas.unique_angle: Reframing schedule failures as data points instead of personal failures

ideas.idea: Video: Stop before you redesign—ask yourself these 3 questions (interrupt the perfection loop before it starts)
ideas.pain_point: Perfectionism loop: redoing systems instead of doing the work
ideas.unique_angle: Teaching metacognition about the urge to redo vs do, not just time management

ideas.idea: Caption-driven post: 'You're not messy, you're a systems tweaker' (normalize it, then give 1 tiny hack to start the work anyway)
ideas.pain_point: Perfectionism loop: redoing systems instead of doing the work
ideas.unique_angle: Validating the personality type while offering a minimal friction intervention

top_picks.idea: Tuesday Breakdown: Why your Sunday plan dies by midweek + what actually sticks
top_picks.reason: Multiple audience members mentioned specific mid-week collapse (Tuesday, Wednesday)—this is a pattern ready to be named and addressed. High relatability, directly actionable.

top_picks.idea: Poll/quiz: 'Is your planner a study tool or a procrastination tool?' + reframe planning as the enemy
top_picks.reason: Directly validates the core doubt in the audience ('does anyone actually stick to a study schedule or is it a scam'). Engagement-driving format with permission to question the premise.

top_picks.idea: The Phone Proximity Problem: practical phone-away setups that don't require willpower
top_picks.reason: Simplest, most universal pain point. Solutions-focused. Avoids the shame of 'just discipline yourself' narrative.

missing_info: What kind of content format performs best on this audience's feed (video, carousel, text post, Reel)?
Do students prefer accountability/community angles or solo-study advice?
What's the actual follow-through rate on study schedules (how many days/weeks do they typically last)?
Are there specific subjects/classes where schedules work better than others?

hooks.text: Your Sunday plan was perfect. Tuesday killed it.
We tracked when your productivity actually dies. It's specific.
You're not lazy. Your planning method just sucks.
90% of college plans fail before Wednesday. Here's why.
Planning on Sunday is your first mistake. Period.
That perfect Sunday plan? Dead by Tuesday morning.
You plan like you care. You don't follow through.
Your planner looks great. Your actual week looks different.
Plot twist: your schedule isn't the problem.
Stop planning Sundays. Start planning like this instead.

winner.text: Your Sunday plan was perfect. Tuesday killed it.
winner.reasoning: This hook mirrors the exact lived experience of procrastinating college students—that specific moment when midweek momentum collapses. The short, punchy sentences feel like a friend calling out the obvious truth, which matches the brand voice and triggers immediate recognition without feeling preachy.

runner_up.text: 90% of college plans fail before Wednesday. Here's why.
runner_up.reasoning: The specific statistic (90%, before Wednesday) adds credibility while the promise of 'here's why' creates a logical curiosity gap. It's slightly safer because it positions the content as explanatory rather than judgmental, appealing to students who want to understand their own failures.

script.script:
[HOOK - 0-3 sec]
[ON-SCREEN TEXT: "Your Sunday plan was perfect."]
[PAUSE 1 sec]
[ON-SCREEN TEXT: "Tuesday killed it."]
[CUT]

[PROBLEM - 3-8 sec]
You know the feeling. You map out your whole week Sunday night. Perfect schedule. Perfect intentions.
[PAUSE]
Then Tuesday hits and you're stress-eating cereal at 2 AM wondering where it all went wrong.
[CUT]

[VALUE - 8-20 sec]
Here's what actually works: Stop planning your whole week.
[PAUSE]
Instead, use the 24-hour block method. Pick ONE day ahead of time. Literally just plan tomorrow.
[ON-SCREEN TEXT: "24-hour blocks > 7-day plans"]
It's specific enough to follow. It's short enough to actually stick to.
[PAUSE]
No overwhelm. No collapse.
[CUT]

[CTA - 20-23 sec]
Want the full system that actually fits how your brain actually works?
[PAUSE]
Follow for the full breakdown.
script.viewer_takeaway: Procrastinators learn that rigid weekly plans fail, but 24-hour planning blocks are manageable and actually work—curiosity drives them to follow for the complete system.

Quick cut to chaotic scene: same person looking disheveled, surrounded by mess, stressed facial expression, low lighting
Cut to person talking directly to camera, casual setting (bedroom/home), relatable hand gestures while speaking about mapping out the week
B-roll montage: person stress-eating cereal at desk, clock showing 2 AM, frustrated head in hands, quick cuts between different collapse moments
Person at desk, emphatically gesturing 'no' at a calendar, then pointing at camera with confident expression, bright background
Split-screen or animated graphic showing: left side = overwhelming 7-day calendar with red marks, right side = single highlighted day in green. Person nods approvingly
Close-up of person's face explaining benefits, natural gestures, pointing to self while saying 'your brain,' conversational tone

frame_plan.on_screen_text: Specific enough to follow. Short enough to stick.
frame_plan.visual_direction: Quick visual of tomorrow's date highlighted on phone/calendar, checkmark appearing, person looking relieved and calm
Person looking directly at camera with friendly smile, hands open in welcoming gesture, call-to-action text appears bottom of screen in brand colors
Quick end-card with brand handle, Instagram follow button graphic, slight zoom or bounce effect

Tuesday chaos: messy desk, unmade bed, scattered papers, dim lighting
2 AM cereal eating: bowl of cereal, spoon, clock showing 2:00, person in sleep clothes
Calendar graphics: 7-day overwhelmed version (red, cluttered), 24-hour clean version (green, organized)
Phone/digital calendar showing tomorrow's date highlighted

B-roll: stressed gestures, head in hands, frustrated facial expressions
Brand color overlays for text and CTA buttons
Instagram follow button graphic for end-card

justifications.clarity: Hook lands immediately with relatable contrast; 24-hour block method is explained in one clear sentence by second 8.
justifications.retention: Stress-eating cereal at 2 AM is specific enough to hold attention, but the value proposition (24-hour blocks) could hit harder emotionally before the pivot.
justifications.save_potential: Clear system with immediate takeaway makes this worth saving; viewers understand the core idea without following yet.
justifications.shareability: Problem is universal but solution lacks novelty—24-hour planning isn't original enough to feel shareable as a 'hack' or revelation.
justifications.audience_fit: Procrastinator pain points (Sunday optimism → Tuesday collapse, 2 AM stress) are precisely mapped to college student experience.
justifications.cta_strength: Follow-for-full-system is clear and low-friction, but 'full breakdown' isn't specific enough to create urgency or curiosity gap.

weaknesses.issue: CTA lacks specificity—'full breakdown' is vague and doesn't create FOMO; followers don't know what they're actually getting.
weaknesses.fix: Rewrite CTA to: 'Follow for the 3-part system that actually stops the Sunday-to-Tuesday collapse (plus a free planning template).'

weaknesses.issue: Shareability is weak because 24-hour blocks feel like incremental advice, not a counterintuitive insight; framing misses the 'aha' moment.
weaknesses.fix: Reframe at 8-sec mark to: 'Stop planning your whole week—it kills motivation. Instead, plan only what you can control: tomorrow. That's it.' (Adds control/agency angle for virality.)

weaknesses.issue: Script doesn't answer 'why 24-hour blocks work'—just that they do; missing the psychological payoff that drives saves.
weaknesses.fix: Add 1-2 sec after 'short enough to stick': 'Because your brain doesn't need 7 days of pressure. It needs 1 day of clarity.' (Reframes as brain science, not tactics.)

captions: Your Sunday plan was flawless. Tuesday had other plans. 📅 The 24-hour block method cuts through the chaos—follow for the full system that actually fits how your brain works (including a free planning template). 🧠
Sunday night energy: 'I've got this.' Tuesday 2 AM energy: *stress eating cereal* 🥣 Stop planning your whole week. Start planning tomorrow. Follow for the breakdown + a system that actually sticks. 🔗
growth.final_call_reason: Strong audience fit and clarity, but shareability and CTA specificity are leaving engagement on the table—tighten the 'why' and replace vague 'full breakdown' with concrete value (template, system components) to lift saves and follows.
